isolated_kernel_timing_a100d.method_fixed: REWRITTEN after phase-4 audit Block 1 (this revision). The ORIGINAL method (below, kept for the record) allocated the CUDA op's own output buffer INSIDE a loop of 50 launches bracketed by exactly ONE trailing `Device::synchronize()` — a 100+ MB fresh `device.alloc` on every one of those 50 calls, with no back-pressure between launches. A re-run on an otherwise-idle a100d found a 2.35x spread across repeats (0.273 / 0.619 / 0.641 / 0.321 ms) purely from that batching/allocator interaction, not the kernel's own cost. FIX (now the crate's only isolated-timing harness, `tests/cuda_parity.rs`'s `time_kernel()`, shared by every `isolated_kernel_timing_*` test so this cannot recur by copy-paste): per-ITERATION `Device::synchronize()` (never one sync batching N launches), >=20 warm-ups, >=200 timed iterations, min AND median reported (fixed fold order, `f64::total_cmp`). `nsys` is unavailable/broken on this pod image (`nsys --version` errors "hasn't been installed with CUDA Toolkit 12.6"), so this stays wall-clock (including per-launch CPU-side dispatch overhead), stated as such rather than implied to be a device-side-only timeline. Neither op's own output-buffer allocation could be hoisted out of the timed region — `apply1`/`apply2` have no output-buffer-reuse entry point in this crate's public surface — so that allocation is still measured on every iteration; it is real device work the harness intentionally reports, not an artifact.
isolated_kernel_timing_a100d.method_original_now_refuted: wall-clock around ONE Device::synchronize() bracketing 50 launches, 1-launch warm-up, release profile — the batching defect described above.
